NOTE 7

In this note we prove that form 43 (Dependent Choice) implies form 113 (A countable product of compact topological spaces is compact.) Our proof is based on the proof of theorem 6.1 in Good/Tree [1995]. Let $\{X_{\alpha }:\alpha <\omega \}$ be a countable set of compact topological spaces. Let $X=\prod _{\alpha \in \omega }X_{\alpha }$ and for $\beta <\omega$ define $p_{\beta }:X\rightarrow \prod _{\alpha \leq \beta }X_{\alpha }$ by $p_{\beta } (x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots ) =(x_{0},\,x_{1},\, \ldots ,\,x_{\beta })$. To show that $X$ is compact let $\mathcal{C}$ be a collection of closed sets in $X$ with the finite intersection property. We will use Dependent Choice to choose a sequence $(x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots )$ with the property that for all $\alpha <\omega ,\,(x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots ,\, x_{\alpha })\in \bigcap \{\overline{p_{\alpha }(C)}:C\in \mathcal{C}\}$. Then we will prove, as in Good/Tree [1995], that $(x_{1},\,x_{2},\,\ldots ) \in \bigcap \mathcal{C}$.

As above, the family $\{X_{\beta +1,\alpha }:\beta <\alpha <\kappa \}$ has the finite intersection property. Since $X_{\beta +1}$ is compact, $\bigcap _{\beta <\alpha <\kappa }X_{\beta +1,\alpha }\neq \emptyset$. Choose $x_{\beta +1}\in \bigcap _{\beta <\alpha <\kappa }X_{\beta +1,\alpha }$.

The argument that $(x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots )$ is in $\bigcap \mathcal{C}$ is by contradiction. Suppose the assertion is false. Then there is an open set $U=\prod _{\alpha <\omega }U_{\alpha }$ and $C\in \mathcal{C}$ such that $(x_{0},\,x_{1},\, \ldots ) \in U$ and $U\cap C=\emptyset$. Choose $\gamma \in \omega$ so that $U_{\alpha }=X_{\alpha }$ whenever $\alpha >\gamma$, and let $V=\prod _{\alpha \leq \gamma }U_{\alpha }$. $V$ is open in $\prod _{\alpha \leq \gamma }X_{\alpha }$. Further $(x_{0},\,x_{1},\,\ldots ,\,x_{\gamma })\in V$ hence $V\cap p_{\gamma }(C)\neq \emptyset$. This means that there is some sequence $(y_{0},\,y_{1},\,\ldots ) \in C$ with $(y_{0},\,y_{1},\,\ldots ,\,y_{\gamma })\in V$. Which (by definition of $V$) implies that $(y_{0},\, y_{1},\,\ldots ) \in U$. This contradicts $U\cap C=\emptyset$.

Until further notice $n\in \omega$ and $Z$ is a finite subset of $\omega$. The first two of the following conditions on the pair $(n,\,Z)$ were introduced by Mostowski in [1958] and the third by Gauntt in [1970].

$D(n,\,Z)$. For any subgroup $G$ of $S_{n}$ (the symmetric group on n) without fixed points, there is a subgroup $H$ of $G$ and proper subgroups $K_{1},\,\ldots ,\,K_{r}$of $H$ such that $\Sigma |H:K_{i}|\in Z$.

$K(n,\,Z)$. For any subgroup $G$ of $S_{n}$ without fixed points, there is a subgroup $H$ of $G^{\omega }$ (the restricted direct product of countably many copies of $G$) and proper subgroups $K_{1},\,\ldots ,\, K_{r}$ of $H$ such that $\Sigma |H:K_{i}|\in Z$

$L(n,\,Z)$. For any subgroup $G$ of $S_{n}$ without fixed points, there are proper subgroups $K_{1},\, \ldots ,\,K_{r}$ of $G$ such that $\Sigma |G:K_{i}|\in Z$.

Blass [1984b] has noticed that $L(n,\,Z)$ is can be formulated as follows:

Every group that can act without fixed points on an $n$ element set can also act without fixed points on a $k$ element set for at least one $k\in Z$.

We now turn to some generalizations of the finite axioms of choice due to Truss [1973a]. Some definitions are necessary. For any set $X$ let $e(X)$ be the set of nonempty finite subsets of $X$ and define $e(0,\, X)=X$ and $e(n+1,\,X)=e(e(n,\,X))$. (We assume that $e(k,\,X) \cap e(j,\,X)=\emptyset$ for $j\neq k$. If this is not the case we replace $e(n,\,X)$ by $\{e(n,\,X)\}\times e(n,\,X)$ for each $n\in \omega$.) Let $V(m,\, X)$ be the set of equivalence classes on $e(m,\,X)$ under the equivalence relation $aRb$ iff $\exists$ a permutation $\phi$ of $X$ such that (the extension of) $\phi (a)=\mathrm{b}$. If $|X|=n\in \omega$ then there is a natural 1-1 correspondence between $V(m,\,n)$ and $V(m,\,X).(\nu \rightarrow f(\nu )$ where $f$ is (the extension of) any one to one correspondence between $X$ and $n$.) For $\nu \in V(m,\,n)$ we denote the corresponding equivalence class in $V(m,\,X)$ by $\nu (X)$. Let $V=\bigcup \{V(m,\,n):m,\,n\in \omega ,\, n\neq 0\}$. For any $Z\subseteq V$, Truss defines the following choice axioms: ($Z$ no longer denotes a finite subset of $\omega$.)

$C(\infty ,\,Z)$. For any set $Y,\,\{\nu (X):\nu \in Z$ and $X\in Y$ and $\nu \in V(m,\,|X|)$ for some $m\in \omega$} has a choice function.

$C(LO,\,Z)$. For any linearly ordered set $Y$, same as above.

$C(WO,\,Z)$. For any well ordered set $Y$, same as above.

If $\nu \in V$, then we let $C(\infty ,\,\nu )$, $C(LO,\,\nu )$ and $C(WO,\,\nu )$ denote respectively $C(\infty ,\,\{\nu \})$, $C(LO,\,\{\nu \})$ and $C(WO,\,\{\nu \})$.

For example, if $Z=\{\nu \}$ where $\nu$ is the set of all pairs of elements of $n$ then $C(\infty ,\, \{\nu \})\equiv C(\infty ,\,\nu )$ is “For every set $Y$ of $n$ elements sets there is a function $f$ such that $\forall X\in Y,\,f(X)$ is a two element subset of X.”

NOTE 19

It is clear that König’s lemma, [10 F] implies [10 K] and using the usual proof that the Completeness Theorem implies the Compactness Theorem, it follows that [10 K] implies [10 L]. To show that [10 L] implies 10, $C(\aleph _{0},\,<\aleph _{0})$, let $X=\{x_{i}: i\in \omega \}$ be a denumerable set of finite sets, where each $x_{i}=\{x_{i,0},\,x_{i,1},\,\cdots x_{i,n_{i}}\}$. Let $\mathcal{L}$ be a first order language with a single function symbol $f$ and constant symbols for each $x_{i}\in X$ and each element $x_{i,j}$ of $\bigcup X$. Let $S$ be the following set of sentence in $\mathcal{L}$: For each $i\in \omega$, the conjunction of

$\wedge (\{x_{i,j}\neq x_{i,k}:j,\,k\leq n_{i}$ and $j\neq k\})$ and

$\vee \,(\{f(x_{i})=x_{i,0},\,\ldots ,\,f(x_{i})=x_{i,n_{i}}\})$.

Each finite subset of $S$ has a model, so [10 L] implies that the denumerable set of sentences has a model. In that model, $f$ is a choice function on $X$.

NOTE 21

Definitions for forms [10 F], [14 M], [14 N], [43 H], [106 A], 216, and 249.

NOTE 22

Definitions for forms [1 L], [1 M], [1 N], [10 C] and [132 A]. A set mapping $f$ is a function $f:X\rightarrow \mathcal{P}(X)$ such that for all $x\in X,\,x\not \in f(x)$. A free subset of $X$ (relative to $f$) is a subset $H$ of $X$ such that for all $x,\,y\in H,\,x\not \in f(y)$. A ramification system is a triple $\langle X,\,E,\,S\rangle$ where $X$ and $E$ are sets and $S\,:\,X^{\leq \theta }\rightarrow \mathcal{P}(E)$ (where $\theta$ is an ordinal and $X^{\leq \theta }$ denotes all functions $t:\alpha \rightarrow X$ where $\alpha \leq \theta$) satisfies (i) $S(\emptyset )=E$ (ii) If $f,\, g\in \mathrm{dom}(S)$ and $f\subseteq g$, then $S(g)\subseteq S(f)$ and (iii) If $f\in \mathrm{dom}(S)$ and $\eta =\mathrm{dom}(f)$ is a limit ordinal then $S(f)=\bigcap _{\alpha <\eta }S(f/\alpha )$.

NOTE 23

Definitions for forms [14 Q] and [52 E]: If $E$ is a Banach space (complete, normed, linear space) then $E^{\ast }$ (the dual of $E$) is the space of all bounded linear functionals on $E$. (That is, all $f:E\rightarrow \,\mathbb{R}$ such that $(\exists M)(\forall x\in E)(|f(x)|\leq \Vert x\Vert M)$. $E^{\ast }$ is a Banach space if we define $\Vert f\Vert =\sup _{x\neq 0}\Big (\frac{|f(x)|}{\Vert x\Vert }\Big )$. Each $x\in E$ can be thought of as a linear functional on $E^{\ast }$ if we define $x(f)=f(x)$ for all $f$ in $E^{\ast }$. The weak$^{\ast }$ topology on $E^{\ast }$ is the weakest topology that makes all these linear functionals continuous. Sets of the form $w_{x,\epsilon }=\{f\in E^{\ast }:|f(x)|<\epsilon \}$ form a basis for this topology. If $X\subseteq E,\,X$ is convex-compact if whenever $F_{i}$, for $i\in I$, are closed convex subsets of $X$ and $\{X\,\cap \,F_{i}:i\in I\}$ has the finite intersection property, then $\bigcap _{i\in I}(X\cap \,F_{i})\neq \emptyset$. Note that the definition of convex-compact may be given in any topological vector space.

Then $W$ (the class of almost well orderable sets) is defined to be $\bigcup \{W(\alpha ):\alpha \in \, On\}$. See Keisler [1970]. Blass [1977b] has shown that If $P\subseteq W$ and $P\in W$, then $\bigcup P\in W$. Regarding the form(s) 179 $(\forall x,\,x\in W(\alpha ))$, R. David [1980] shows that for ordinals $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with $0<\alpha <\beta$, the statement $\forall x,\,x\in W(\beta )$ does not imply $\forall x,\,x\in W(\alpha )$. (Clearly, $\forall x,\,x\in W(\alpha )$ implies $\forall x,\,x\in W(\beta ).)$ It is clear that 30 + 294 (every linearly ordered $W$-set can be well ordered) implies that every $W$-set can be well ordered. Thus, 30 + 294 + 144 (every set is a $W$-set) implies AC.

NOTE 26

A summary of the definitions and results from Brunner [1983a]. Brunner considers 16 properties a topological space $(X,\,\underline{X})$ may have:

W1

: $\underline{X}$ is w.o. (well ordered);

W2

: $X$ is w.o.;

D1

: $X$ is covered by a w.o. family of closed, discrete sets.

D2

: $X$ is covered by a w.o. family of discrete sets;

B1

: $X$ has a w.o. base

B2

: $\exists f:X\times W\rightarrow \underline{X}$ such that $W$ is w.o. and $f^{\prime }\{x\}\times W)$ is a neighborhood base at $x$ for each $x\in X$.

B3

: $\exists f:X\times W\rightarrow \underline{X}$ such that $W$ is w.o. and $\forall x\in X,\,\{x\}=\bigcap f^{\prime }\{x\}\times W)$

L1

: Each open cover of $X$ has a w.o. subcover;

L2

: Each open cover of $X$ has a w.o. refinement;

S

: $X$ has a dense, w.o. subset;

C

: Each family $O\subseteq \underline{X}$ of pairwise disjoint sets is w.o.

A1

: If $O\subseteq \underline{X}$ covers $X,\,\exists f:X\rightarrow O$ such that $\forall x\in X,\, x\in f(x)$;

A2

: If $O\subseteq \underline{X}$ covers $X,\,\exists f:X\rightarrow \underline{X}$ s.t. $\forall x\in X,\,x\in f(x)$ and $f^{\prime }X$ refines $O$;

H1

: $X$ is hereditarily $A1$;

H2

: $X$ is hereditarily $A2$;

F

: $X$ is a continuous finite to one image of an $A1$ space.

All of the $A(P)$’s occur in the list of forms, but not all the $A(P,\,Q)$’s occur.

The table below, taken from Brunner [1983a], summarizes the results. In the table, $0$ means that $A(P,\, Q)$ ($P$ the row heading and $Q$ the column heading) is provable in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$. $N$ means $A(P,\,Q)$ is not provable in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$. $AC$ (form 1), $MC$ (form 67) and $PW$ (form 91) mean respectively that $A(P,\,Q)$ is equivalent to $AC,\,MC$ or $PW$ in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$. And $IMC$ or $IPW$ mean that $A(P,\,Q)$ implies $MC$ or $PW$ respectively in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$.
